opener.heading: Week 29: Ice Cream & Summer Treats 🍦
about: Everything this week is cold and she makes most of it herself. Friday she shakes cream and salted ice in a bag for ten minutes and eats the result out of the bag. That afternoon five ice cubes go into five wrappings, and she opens all of them every twenty minutes to see which one is still there at dinner. Thursday runs the same idea long: a fork dragged across a freezing tray every half hour from half past nine in the morning.

Between those two ends the week turns outward. She marks where the hatch goes in a big box on Saturday, you cut it, and she serves you from behind it. She builds a sundae to everybody's order on Sunday, and freezes a pot for each person on Monday with the flavor picked from something she has noticed about them. Tuesday the stroller becomes a van and the whole house moves when she rings and stops when she stops. Wednesday she names eight people who did something for her this week and rolls each name inside a paper cone. Nothing lands on the calendar, so the heat sets the shape: kitchen in the morning, shade or water after lunch.
azlyn: Salt makes ice colder than ice. She shakes a bag of cream buried in salted ice and eats ice cream out of it ten minutes later.
What keeps cold in. Foil, a dish towel, shredded paper in a lidded box, a bowl of water, bare on a saucer. She predicts first, then checks every twenty minutes.
Waiting, counted down. Eight pegs come off a string one at a time while the granita freezes, so half an hour turns into something she can see.
Taking an order and giving change. She runs the hatch of a cardboard shop, hands out the jobs, then swaps sides and lines up as the customer.
Saying what she has noticed about a person. Four frozen pots and eight paper cones, each carrying one name and one reason in her own words.
you: Celebration is a legitimate way to teach history
Children describe parents by what they do, not who they are
Food is the most durable carrier of family memory
Admiration is how children choose which traits to grow
Moving in time with someone builds connection, measurably
Gratitude needs a target before it needs a feeling
Waiting is easier when it's visible and shrinking
shopping: Ice cube trays, every one you own, filled and frozen from Thursday night
Table salt, a full box (6 tbsp goes into the ice on Friday)
Heavy cream or whole milk, 2/3 cup (150 ml)
Canned peaches or other canned fruit, plus whatever fresh fruit is in
Chocolate sauce, or cocoa to mix with sugar
Index cards, 12, or a cereal box to cut up
1 large cardboard box, tall enough for her to stand behind
3 flattened cardboard boxes, for the menu board, the van sign and the coins
1 cookie tin, or a second shoebox
A craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
4 small pots or cups with lids
4 tall plastic beakers and 4 long spoons
1 shallow metal or plastic tray for the granita
A lidded tub for the berry picking
Sun cream and a sun hat each
A laundry basket, or the stroller
A timer, on the stove or your phone
Two cleared freezer shelves, one of them flat
Old family photos, if any are to hand
Something real to serve through the shop hatch on Saturday afternoon
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 13 months this week. He walks, climbs anything with a lip on it, and carries things from room to room while he moves.

days.title: Ice Cream Without a Freezer
days.prepTonight: Freeze every ice tray you own and stand the cream, the salt and both sizes of zip-seal bag on the counter. Saturday needs a box she can stand behind.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Ice Cube Race on the Step

opening.title: Filling the Cold Bag
opening.need: 1 large zip-seal freezer bag · a tray of ice cubes · 6 tbsp table salt · 1 tablespoon · masking tape and a marker.
steps: She loads ice into the big bag by the handful until it is half full. It sticks to wet fingers and she will refuse help.
Six tablespoons of salt go in on top. She spoons, you count out loud.
Seal it, tape a strip across the front and write COLD BAG on it. Tell her the salt is doing something to that ice, and she finds out at 9:15.

main.title: Ten Minutes of Shaking
materials: 2/3 cup heavy cream or whole milk (150 ml)
Ice cubes to half-fill the big bag
steps: Pour the cream into the small bag. She adds the sugar and a drop of vanilla, and smells it first.
Press the bag flat on the table to push the air out, seal it and tape along the seal. Trapped air splits it later.
Open the cold bag, bury the small bag in the ice and salt, and seal it again.
Wrap the dish towel round the parcel and shake. Sing something with a long chorus, hand it over, take it back when her arms go.
At five minutes she presses a finger on the small bag through the towel. It sets at the edges before the middle.
At ten, lift it out, wipe the salt off with the towel, open it and eat out of the bag with the two spoons.
main.tip: Her arms give out long before the ten minutes do. Count the swaps out loud as you pass it back and forth.

outside.title: The Ice Cube Race on the Step
paras: Take four cubes out to the front step on a plate at half past ten, after three hours of July sun on the paving. Two go on the hot slab, two in the shade of the wall. The hot pair is water before you finish talking about it. Put the back of your hand on each slab, then let her put hers on both, and give her one second of a bare foot on the sunny one only if you could hold your own hand there.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and carrying things while he walks is his project this month. Put your hands over his round the wrapped parcel for two or three shakes. Outside, stand him barefoot on the shaded slab and keep him on it, because the sunny slab has had three hours of July on it.

second.title: Keeping One Cube Till Dinner
second.intro: Five ice cubes go into five wrappings at one o'clock, and one has to last until dinner.
materials: A clock or a phone timer
steps: Tear five strips of tape, number them 1 to 5 with the marker, and she sticks one on each saucer.

Cube 1 sits bare. Cube 2 goes in the folded dish towel, cube 3 in foil, cube 4 buried in shredded newspaper inside the lidded shoebox, cube 5 into the bowl of water. Each stands on its numbered saucer.
Line them up out of the sun. Ask which wins, write all five numbers on a sixth strip of tape stuck to the wall and circle the one she picks to win.
Set the timer for twenty minutes. Each time it goes she opens all five and you cross the dead ones off the wall strip. Leave the kitchen in between, because the timer is what brings her back.
Around three, tell her where this comes from. Men sawed blocks out of frozen lakes in winter, packed them in straw inside a thick-walled ice house and sold that ice in August.
Whichever cube reaches six o'clock goes in a drink at the table, and she names the winner.
second.tip: The bowl of water goes first and she will argue. Water carries heat into a cube faster than air does.

alternatives: Two cubes only, one bare and one in the dish towel.
Ice cubes and a slotted spoon in warm water.
Juice cubes to draw on paper with.
outAgain: Meet a friend at the park, late enough that the metal has cooled
The shady end of the green with a blanket and cold water
The splash pad, if it is running this week
A friend's garden, for a hose and a shaded step

aroundWorld.title: Frozen Treats Everywhere 🍧
paras: People ate frozen candy long before anyone had a freezer. Iranian cooks made faloodeh, thin frozen noodles in rose water and lime, from ice kept underground all summer in a yakhchāl. Sicily has granita, Mexico sells paletas from street carts, and Japan shaves ice into a soft mountain called kakigōri.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Squeeze half a lemon into a cup of apple juice, freeze it and scrape it with a fork. That is granita, and Azlyn makes a tray on Thursday.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Persian ice houses were built 2,400 years ago and kept ice through desert summers.

days.krestonPM: He goes to the park on his feet rather than in the stroller. Grass at 13 months is uneven and grabs at his shoes, so he staggers the first few steps and then works it out. Give him one thing to carry the whole way.

insight.headline: Celebration is a legitimate way to teach history.
paras: Azlyn cannot hold "before freezers" as a fact. She can hold an afternoon where she wrapped five ice cubes five different ways and one of them lasted until dinner, and the fact rides along inside the memory. Museum educators lean on the same move: give her the practice, the food, the object in her hand, and the dates arrive years later with somewhere to land. She shook a bag for ten minutes to earn one bowl of ice cream, so she knows something true now about what a cold sweet used to cost. Make the treat, eat it, say who else made it this way.

days.safety: Ice packed in salt drops well below freezing and burns bare skin faster than plain ice does. The parcel stays inside the dish towel and never rests against her arm. Put the back of your hand on the sunny slab before either of them stands on it. If you cannot hold it there, it comes off bare feet and Kreston stays on the shaded side. Loose cubes and spilled salt come off the floor straight away: Kreston walks at 13 months, and a cube he finds is a choking risk. Mid-July sun off a front step burns in twenty minutes, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Ice Cream Shop
days.prepTonight: Stand the big box upright in the front room with the marker and tape on top, and put a tub of ice cream in the freezer for tomorrow.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Hatch in the Big Box

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Chalk Menu on the Path

opening.title: Six Flavors and a Sign
steps: Ask her for six flavors. Write them word for word and give the invented ones the same weight as the real ones.
She draws a scoop beside each name in whatever color that flavor is to her.
Read the six back in a shop voice, loud. That paper is the menu and it goes on the board at 9:15.

main.title: The Hatch in the Big Box
materials: 1 large cardboard box, tall enough to stand behind
1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
1 flattened box for the menu board
Cardboard circles cut as coins, palm-sized
steps: Stand her behind the box and mark the hatch with tape at her chest height, wide enough for a tray. Cut it with her standing back, and say why.
Roll the ten sheets into cones. She rolls, you tape the seam, and the wonky ones stay in the pile.
Scrunch newspaper into balls, two scoops a cone. She will make forty of them.
Lay the flattened box down for the menu board and tape this morning's menu sheet to the middle of it. She copies the scoops bigger around the edge in crayon.
Cut the cardboard coins palm-sized, so nothing small reaches the floor. She draws a number on each.
Prop the board against the box, stand behind the hatch and buy something off her. Pay with a coin, wait for change.
main.tip: Cut the hatch narrow. A wide one turns the box into a doorway she walks through.

outside.title: The Chalk Menu on the Path
paras: Take the chalk to the sidewalk outside the front door and let her write the shop's name across it, the flavors underneath and prices she invents. Third week of July, so work in whatever shade the house throws. Anyone walking past gets the menu read at them.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and a chalk stub goes straight to his mouth, so keep it in your own hand with his fingers over yours and let him scrub it on the paving between Azlyn's letters. Keep him on the house side of the path, hat on, and put the back of your hand on the paving before he sits down on it.

second.title: The Jobs She Hands Out
second.intro: The shop opens at one o'clock with staff, and the rule is that you take the job she gives you.
materials: The box shop and the menu board
1 bell, or a saucepan lid and a spoon
A real snack to serve at 3:30
steps: Tuck the dish towel into her waistband as an apron. She rings the bell, or bangs the lid with the spoon, and the shop is open.
She hands out jobs: who scoops, who pays, who carries the tray. Take yours without negotiating.
Everybody lines up with coins and orders off the board. She serves two paper scoops a cone, takes the money and hands back nonsense change. Let it be nonsense.
Swap over. She becomes the customer, you run a bad shop and get her order wrong.
Sit her down with the crayons and the marker to draw each person doing their job on the side of the box. Write the names where she says.
At half past three the real snack goes through the hatch on the tray, and the shop does a round with real food in it.
Leave it standing. She is behind that counter again at quarter past four with nobody watching.
second.tip: She will hand you the dull job on purpose. Line up, complain about the wait, order two scoops of something she invented.

alternatives: Serve out of the stroller in the yard and skip the box.
Draw the menu on the window with washable pens.
Open a shop that sells the toys she is bored of.
outAgain: The pet shop and then the garden center, fish tanks first, plants after
The garden center on its own, for the café and the sprinklers
The park with a friend, if the heat has broken
A supermarket freezer aisle and one thing she picks
Home and the sprinkler
days.krestonPM: The fish tanks are the whole trip for him at 13 months. Hold him at glass height and stay there while he watches. In the garden center let him walk a wide aisle holding one finger. He stops at every low shelf, and the herbs are worth a touch.

insight.headline: Children describe parents by what they do, not who they are.
paras: Ask a three-year-old about her mother and you get she makes the toast and she does my hair. Azlyn built you out of actions, because actions are the part she can see, and the shop lets her hand them back out. Watch which job she gives you. The person she puts on the register is the one she has filed as the one who sorts things out, and the drawing on the side of the box will tell you the same. Her picture of you is a list of what you do all day, worth knowing on days when that list feels invisible.

days.safety: The craft knife cuts the hatch and goes back out of reach between cuts, not onto the arm of the sofa. Check inside the box for staples before either child gets near it. Kreston climbs at 13 months, so weight the box down or lay it flat whenever he is loose and you are not beside him. The chalk menu goes on an open sidewalk in the third week of July, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Sundae with Everybody In It
days.prepTonight: Stand the four beakers and the long spoons by the sink, check there are two bananas, and clear a freezer shelf for tomorrow.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Tallest Glass in the House

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Forks and the Long Spoons

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Long Bath and the Cold Drink

opening.title: The Pudding Joseph Remembers
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 pen · everybody who is in the house.
steps: Ask Joseph what he ate on hot days when he was small. Let him take his time over the detail, because the detail is the part she repeats later.
She asks everyone else the same question in her own words.
Write the answers down with a name beside each. That list sits on the table until 9:15.

main.title: The Tallest Glass in the House
materials: 1 tub of ice cream, or Friday's
4 tall plastic beakers and 4 long spoons
A handful of cookies and 1 bag to crush them in
Jam, loosened with a spoon of hot water
Chocolate sauce, or cocoa and sugar
1 index card or cut cereal-box card, and 1 pen
steps: Stand the four beakers in a row. Everybody names one layer and she goes round asking. Write each name and layer on the card in order.
She breaks the bananas up with her hands. No knife, and the pieces will be huge.
Cookies into the bag, and she crushes them with her fist against the table.
Loosen the jam with a spoon of hot water yourself and leave it to cool. Cocoa stirred into sugar with a splash of hot water makes the chocolate sauce if there is none in.
Build all four in the order on the card, a scoop of ice cream under each new layer and the canned fruit where the card says. Her hands, your steadying.
Photograph the card next to the beakers before anyone eats, then hand out the long spoons.
main.tip: Her running order is final. Three layers of jam and no fruit is a recipe, and it goes on the card.

outside.title: Berries for the Top
paras: Walk to whatever fruit is ripe within stroller distance in the third week of July. Raspberries on somebody's fence, mulberries down under the tree, the first blackberries if the summer has run warm. She picks into a lidded tub and carries more than she eats, because none of it gets eaten until it is washed at home, and the rest goes in the freezer for tomorrow's pots.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and posts what he picks straight into his mouth, so his share waits until the tub has been through the sink at home. Raspberries and mulberries are soft enough then, squashed between your fingers first. Give him his own empty tub to carry and expect it upended at least once. He wants the walk on his feet, so plan on carrying him home.

second.title: The Tin by the Cookbooks
second.intro: Clear the table after lunch and fill in four cards, then put them in a tin that stays in this kitchen for years.
materials: 8–10 index cards or cut cereal-box card
Old photos, if any are to hand
A phone to photograph each card
steps: One card in front of her at a time. She answers out loud and you write it down.
Card one: what Joseph ate on hot days when he was small, from this morning. Card two: what gets made in this house at birthdays.
Card three: what Brooklyn's family ate that nobody makes now. Card four: the food she wants to be hers, the one people will say is her thing.
She draws on the back of each. Her drawing is the part she will recognize in ten years.
This morning's recipe card joins the pile.
Spread out any old photos to hand. She names who is in them and dictates a line about each onto a card.
Tape a label on the tin and write what she calls it. Photograph every card, then the tin goes on the shelf with the cookbooks.
second.tip: Write what she says, mistakes and all. A card reading strawbrees is worth ten tidy ones.

alternatives: One card only, the birthday one.
Ring a grandparent and ask them the same question.
Draw this morning's sundae instead of writing anything.
outAgain: A nature hunt walk, five things to find: something furry, something dry, something that smells
The shaded woods path, for the temperature drop under the trees
The duck pond, late enough that the light has gone gold
A short walk after six, if the afternoon has been too hot to move
days.krestonPM: Take him on the hunt on foot and let him set the pace, which at 13 months is twenty yards in ten minutes with a stop at every drain. Give him the tub to carry. He picks up whatever is under his feet and hands it to Azlyn.

insight.headline: Food is the most durable carrier of family memory.
paras: Ask an adult what their grandmother's kitchen smelled like and the answer comes back fast. Smell runs straight to the memory and emotion centers of the brain and taste rides along with it, so a food memory arrives whole and lands before any of the words do. Azlyn will lose almost all of this year to the ordinary forgetting of being three. She keeps the sundae with everybody's layer in it, on the condition that you make it again, because repetition turns one afternoon into a tradition. The tin covers your memory as well as hers: the recipes you are certain you could never forget are the first to go.

days.safety: No nuts, no whole grapes and no hard sprinkles anywhere near Kreston at 13 months. His fruit is mashed and his portion is soft. Only pick what you can name. Anything you are not certain of stays on the bush, and nothing goes in Kreston's mouth unwashed. Jam loosened with hot water scalds, so it cools before she touches it. Plastic beakers rather than glass, and nothing sweet left at his height. A picking walk at eleven has no shade in it, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: A Flavor Named After You
days.prepTonight: Clear a whole freezer shelf, stand the four pots and their lids by the kettle, and move the yogurt to the front of the fridge.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Fishing the Ice Out of the Paddling Pool

opening.title: One Thing They Do
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 pen · masking tape.
steps: Write the name of everyone in the house down the page, one under the other, and read the four out.
Ask her one thing each person does. Actions, so he carries me upstairs rather than he is kind. Write it word for word.
Tape the list to the fridge at her height. The four pots at 9:15 take their names off it.

main.title: Four Pots, Four Names
materials: 2 cups plain yogurt (500 g), or 1 tub of vanilla ice cream, softened
4 small pots or cups with lids
Mix-ins from the cabinet: jam, crushed cookie, cocoa, banana, canned peaches, sprinkles, Sunday's frozen berries
steps: Split the yogurt between the four pots with the spoon. She scrapes, and the four will not come out even.
Line the mix-ins along the table and read the fridge list out. One pot per name.
For each pot she picks what that person would want and says why out loud. Take the reason as it comes, including because he is loud.
She mashes each pot with the fork, one at a time, and the fork gets wiped in between or all four taste the same.
Tape a label on every lid: the name, and her reason underneath in her words.
Lids on and onto the cleared shelf, front row where she can see them. They come out at one o'clock, firm at the edge and soft in the middle.
main.tip: Veto nothing. Cocoa with canned peaches is a decision she made about a person, and she is watching whether her reasons count.

outside.title: Fishing the Ice Out of the Paddling Pool
paras: Set the pool up in the shade with three inches of water and tip a tray of ice cubes in. She goes in barefoot and fishes them out by hand, counting them into a cup on the grass, and the game ends when the last one is caught or melted. The pool goes over the flowerbed after.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and the pool floor is the hardest surface he has stood on, slick and shifting under him. He drops to sitting inside a minute and slaps the water flat-handed for a long time after that. Sit in with him and float a bath toy where his hands are. He watches Azlyn chase the cubes with the bath toy in his own hands, and the cubes stay on her side of the pool.

second.title: Which One Is Yours
second.intro: The pots come out at one o'clock and nobody is told which is theirs. Everybody tastes with their eyes shut and guesses.
materials: 1 dish towel for the eyes-shut turns
1 pitcher of water and paper towels
steps: Bring the pots out and turn the lids face down so nobody reads a label early.
Everyone takes a turn with the dish towel over their eyes and a clean teaspoon, tasting all four.
A mouthful of water from the pitcher between tastes, paper towels for the chins.
Each person guesses which pot was made for them. She keeps score on her fingers and gets the count wrong.
Read the labels out. The reason is the part she wants heard, so let her say her own words back with you.
She rolls the four sheets into cones and tapes the seams. You write the flavor name and her reason inside each with the marker, and she covers the outside in crayon.
One cone handed to each person, and whatever is left of the pots goes back in the freezer.
second.tip: Everybody guesses wrong and that is the good bit. Hearing I thought that one was mine tells her the flavors carry something.

alternatives: Two pots instead of four, hers and one other.
Taste-test four juices with eyes shut and rank them.
Draw the four labels as portraits and stop there.
outAgain: The playground with the big slide, checked with your palm first because the metal has been in the sun since seven
The park with the most shade, whichever one that is
The green with a ball and a bottle of water each
The riverside path, for the cool coming off the water
days.krestonPM: At 13 months he climbs anything with a lip on it, so the toddler frame steps are his whole afternoon. Let him go up, stay a hand's width behind, and count the tries. He goes down the short toddler slide on his own, sitting up and feet first, with you standing at the bottom, and he wants it again the second he lands, pointing rather than crying, which is new.

insight.headline: Admiration is how children choose which traits to grow.
paras: Azlyn is watching the three of you and deciding which bits to keep. She made a pot for each of you this morning out of one noticed thing, and the noticing came first. Children build themselves out of the adults nearest to them, and the traits they copy are the ones they have heard named out loud and approved. Say what you admire in front of her and name the person: Daddy fixes things nobody asks him to fix. She files it. The fridge list records what she has picked up already, and it is worth reading twice before it comes down.

days.safety: Standing water is the day's hazard. A 13-month-old who walks can drown in the few inches of a paddling pool, in silence and in seconds, so Kreston stays within arm's reach the whole time and the pool gets tipped out the moment you go indoors. The ice stays in Azlyn's half, counted out and counted back in, because a cube in his fist goes to his mouth. Nobody rides a slide with him on a lap, at any age: his shoe catches on the bed, the leg twists, and your weight finishes the break. He goes down the short toddler slide alone, with an adult at the bottom. The pool goes up in the open at half past ten, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Ice Cream Van
days.prepTonight: Empty the laundry basket and stand it by the front door with a flattened box, the marker and a saucepan lid on top of it.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Three Sounds the Van Makes

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Van That Comes Down Our Street

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Passing the Cone on the Beat

opening.title: The Three Sounds the Van Makes
opening.need: 1 metal spoon · 1 saucepan lid · her voice.
steps: Ask what an ice cream van sounds like. Get three sounds out of her: the chime, the engine idling, the hatch sliding open.
She makes each one with her mouth and you copy her, wrong enough that she corrects you.
Settle the chime: three hits of the spoon on the lid, the same three every time. That is the signal for the rest of the day.

main.title: The Van That Comes Down Our Street
materials: 1 flattened cardboard box for the sign
1 bell, or the metal spoon and saucepan lid
The paper scoops from Saturday, or fresh newspaper
steps: Tape the flattened box to the front of the stroller or the side of the basket. She says what the sign says and you write it big.
Load the van: eight paper cups, the paper scoops, the tray laid across the top.
Chalk three stops on the floor if it is tile or vinyl, tape three crosses if it is carpet. She chooses where they go and one of them will be daft.
She pushes, you follow, and the chime rings the whole way. At each stop everybody stops dead and she serves whoever is standing there.
The rule for the round: moving while the chime rings, still when it stops. Vary how long you leave the silence.
Swap over. You push and she rings, which is the harder job, because the person holding the chime decides when everybody else moves.
main.tip: Stopping dead is the part she cannot do and wants to practice. Give her the bell for the last ten minutes and let her catch you moving.

outside.title: Three Stops and a Bell
paras: Take the round out to the sidewalk. Chalk three stops along the path: one at the gate, one further than she expects, one at the corner. Then walk the loop with the bell going. Twenty past ten in late July is warm enough that the asphalt smells of it. Serve a cup of water at every stop and let her ring at the neighbor's gate.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and walks the sidewalk round on his own feet, one hand on the rim of the van and one on your finger. He stops at every chalked stop and every gate, so let the round run at his pace. Hat on, and he stays on the house side of you the whole loop.

second.title: Passing the Cone on the Beat
second.intro: Everybody sits down for this one. One paper cone goes round a circle on a beat she controls by the end of it.
materials: 1 bell, or the spoon and saucepan lid
A phone with music on it
1 dish towel for the eyes-shut rounds
steps: Cushions in a circle on the floor, everyone sitting close enough to pass without leaning.
Tap the lid at walking pace. The cone moves one person per tap and nobody runs ahead of the beat.
Speed it up until it falls apart, then slow it down to something almost too slow to sit through. She calls fast or slow.
Music on the phone instead of the beat. The music stops and whoever holds the cone names a flavor, and no flavor twice.
Eyes-shut round. Dish towel over her eyes, and she passes and receives by feel while everyone stays quiet.
Hand her the bell. She sets the tempo and the whole circle moves to her hand, which she will test to destruction.
Last round: say the name of the person you are passing to.
second.tip: Nobody goes out and nobody wins. The cone stopping on her is the pleasure, and it evaporates the moment there is a loser in the circle.

alternatives: Pass a cushion instead and skip the beat.
Musical statues with the same three-hit chime.
Everyone copies her rhythm on saucepan lids, one at a time.
outAgain: Swimming, and the coolest hour of the day
The splash pad if the pool is full of the holiday crowd
The shallow end for twenty minutes and home again
A shaded park and a cold drink, if the pool is shut
days.krestonPM: He is in the water too. At 13 months he walks the shallow end holding both your hands and pushes against the drag, which is hard work and he will do it until he is cold. Twenty-five minutes is plenty. Get him out while he is still enjoying it and feed him inside the half hour.

insight.headline: Moving in time with someone builds connection, measurably.
paras: Rocking a baby in time with your own breathing, clapping a rhythm, walking in step: children who move in synchrony with an adult go on to help that adult more and share with them more, and the effect shows up in four-year-olds in the lab within minutes of a shared beat. Azlyn passing a cone round a circle on your tap is doing something older than any of the words in it. She is matching her timing to everybody else in the circle and feeling what that is like. On a day when she has been contrary since breakfast, a shared rhythm resets more than a conversation will.

days.safety: An adult keeps a hand on the stroller out on the sidewalk, whoever is doing the pushing, and the round stays this side of the curb. At the pool Kreston is within arm's reach every second he is in the water, and armbands are not a substitute for your hands. Kreston walks the round on his own feet and goes faster than he can stop, so he stays on the house side of you the whole loop with one hand on the van and one on your finger. The sidewalk round runs in open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: Thank You, In a Cone
days.prepTonight: Put eight sheets of paper and the pens on the table, leave whatever is left of Monday's pots in the freezer, and buy juice or a watermelon for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The List of Who Did Something

opening.title: The List of Who Did Something
steps: Ask who has done something for her this week. Prompt with the specifics: who built the shop, who drove to swimming, who carried her home.
Keep going until there are eight names. The neighbor counts, the woman at the library counts, Kreston counts.
Write what each one did beside the name, in her words. The eight cones at 9:15 come straight off this list.

main.title: The Cones with Names Inside
materials: 1 paper bag to carry them in
steps: Lay a sheet flat. Write the first name from the list she made at eight across the top with the marker and her reason underneath in her words.
She turns it over and draws a scoop on the back in that person's color, felt pens or crayons as she likes.
Roll it so the writing ends up inside, tape the seam, and trim the top edge level. The scissors are yours and go back on the shelf between cones.
Work down the list. At four cones, offer to leave the rest until after lunch and take her answer as given.
Stand the finished ones along the windowsill. Eight of anything in a row is worth looking at.
Two go in the paper bag for the mail slots at half past ten, and she picks which two.
main.tip: She will read the inside out loud as she hands it over. Let her, and write the line in anyway. It is there for the person to find on their own later.

outside.title: The Two Nearest Mail Slots
paras: Walk the two cones to the two nearest doors on her list. Press the seam flat and they go through a mail slot, or knock and hand it over if the person is the sort who will come out. Late July and school has broken up, so somebody will be in a garden and the walk will take twice as long as it should.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and a mail slot flap is the best posting slot he has met. Hold the flap open and let him push the second cone through. He will let go too early and want it back, so keep one hand on it. Walking with something in his fist and giving it up on purpose are two different jobs, and he is halfway through the second.

second.title: The Sundae She Doesn't Eat
second.intro: One bowl gets made this afternoon for somebody who is out of the house, and it waits in the freezer with a place set at the table.
materials: Ice cream, or a leftover pot from Monday
1 topping she chooses for that person
1 spoon, a scrap of paper and masking tape for the flag
Freezer space at the front of a shelf
steps: Read the morning list back and let her pick the one person who did the most. Take her choice even when it is the wrong one by your accounting.
She builds the bowl: ice cream or Monday's pot, and the one topping she says that person likes best.
Lid on and into the front of the freezer. Nobody tastes it, and that includes her.
She writes the name on the card, or dictates it and decorates the edges.
Tape the scrap of paper to the spoon as a flag and lay the spoon across the card.
Set the place at the table: card, spoon, flag, chair pulled out. It stays set through dinner.
She fetches it when they walk in and says the reason out loud.
second.tip: Make her a second bowl if the waiting turns painful. Today is about handing something over, and she can do that with a spoon in her own mouth.

alternatives: One cone for one person, posted, and nothing else.
Draw the person doing the thing they did, instead of writing it.
Phone somebody on the list and let her say it out loud.
outAgain: The library, the every two weeks one, and the coolest building she will stand in today
Indoor playground, if the library is full of the holiday crowd
The store, and she carries one thing
The park on the way home, in the shade at the far end
days.krestonPM: Take him to the board-book corner and put him down. At 13 months he walks the shelves with one hand out, pulling books off as he goes, and putting them back is your job rather than his. Let Azlyn choose one for him and carry it to the desk. He will hold it the whole way home.

insight.headline: Gratitude needs a target before it needs a feeling.
paras: Telling a three-year-old to be grateful gets you a flat thank you aimed at nobody. Azlyn spent this morning naming eight people and what each of them did, which is the part that does the work. Gratitude research keeps landing in the same place: the benefit lands when a person can say who helped, what they did and what it cost them. She cannot hold all three yet, so she practices the first two with a cone in her hand and a name written inside it. Ask her who did something today at dinner and you get a real answer, which is the habit underneath the feeling.

days.safety: The scissors are the only hazard on the table and they cut paper faster than anything she has used. They come out for the trim and go back on a high shelf between cones, never left down while Kreston is walking the room. The walk to the two doors runs at half past ten in late July, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Treat That Takes All Day
days.prepTonight: Clear a flat freezer shelf and stand the tray, the juice, the sugar, a lemon, the string and eight pegs on the counter.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Eight Pegs, Off the Line

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: A Cool Bath and Three Books

opening.title: Sweet Enough to Freeze
opening.need: the juice · 2 cups · 1 tsp sugar · half a lemon · 1 spoon.
steps: The juice you stood on the counter last night is the morning's whole supply. Pour a little into each cup, the same amount in both, and leave the rest, 1 2/3 cups of it, for 9:15.
Stir the teaspoon of sugar and a squeeze of lemon into the second cup until the grains are gone.
She tastes both and calls which is sweeter. Tell her sweet water freezes soft enough to scrape and plain water freezes into a brick, and the tray goes in at 9:15.

main.title: The Tray That Gets Scraped
materials: 1 2/3 cups juice or blitzed watermelon (400 ml)
steps: Stir the sugar and the juice of the half lemon into the 1 2/3 cups until no grains are left on the bottom. She stirs, you check.
Pour it into the tray, a finger deep and no deeper, and she carries it flat to the cleared shelf.
Tape one end of the string to the fridge and the other to a cupboard handle, pulled taut at her height. She clips all eight pegs along it.
Write READY on a strip of tape and stick it past the last peg, so the end of the line is a place.
Every half hour from half past nine, open the freezer and drag the fork across the tray, breaking the frozen edges into the middle. She takes one peg off each time.
Two pegs are still on the line at lunch. Leave them.
main.tip: Scrape, do not stir. Dragging the fork across the top makes crystals; stirring makes slush that sets solid.

outside.title: Watermelon on the Back Step
paras: Cut a watermelon into wedges and eat it on the back step, all of you, juice down wrists. Spit the seeds at a target on a tray set down in front of the step. Thursday in late July is hot, so the fruit comes out of the fridge cold. The rinds go out for the birds.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and a wedge with the rind left on is a handle he can manage. He sits on the step to eat it and stays sitting, both hands busy. He will suck it dry, drop it, and hold his hand out for the next one.

second.title: The Last Peg Comes Off
second.intro: Lay the table at one o'clock for the end of the week. She takes the final peg off the line herself and serves what has been in the freezer since 9:15.
materials: The granita tray and the peg line
Cups or beakers and teaspoons for everybody
1 sheet of paper and 1 pen for the ranking
The week's photos on a phone
Whatever is left of the week's flavors and cones
steps: Lay the sheet over the table and let her set it out: cups, teaspoons, the leftover cones stood down the middle.
Call everybody in. She goes to the line and takes the last peg off in front of them.
Fork the tray one more time and serve it into the cups. His is scraped fine and slushy and goes to him sitting down, and what is left of the week's flavors comes out beside it.
She names the week's treats down the sheet of paper while you write them, one line each.
Everybody votes best and worst out loud, and she marks the votes with the pen. The count will not add up.
Go through the week's photos on the phone and let her narrate them: the shaking, the shop, the sundae, the van.
The ranking sheet goes into the recipe tin with Sunday's cards.
second.tip: Serve the adults a proper cupful. She has watched this tray all day.

alternatives: Serve it in the yard and skip the table.
Four pegs instead of eight and eat it after lunch.
Rank the week in drawings instead of words.
outAgain: The garden center, for the watering cans and the cold glasshouse smell
The hardware store, if the garden center is a drive too far
The duck pond, with the watermelon rind left at home
The green space with a ball, once the sun is off it
days.krestonPM: At 13 months the garden center is a wide flat floor with things at his height. Let him walk the main aisle and stop at the low trays. He carries something the whole way round and hands it to a member of staff, so pick it yourself.

insight.headline: Waiting is easier when it's visible and shrinking.
paras: Azlyn has no working sense of half an hour. Eight pegs on a string give her one, because the line gets shorter in front of her and she is the one taking them off. Children wait longer and complain less when the wait is represented by something they can see and act on, which is why sticker charts work and soon does not. The wait also gets easier when she has a job inside it, and the fork scrape is that job. Use the same trick on car journeys and doctors' waiting rooms: something countable, going down, in her hands.

days.safety: Hard chunks of ice are a choking hazard for Kreston at 13 months, so his portion is scraped fine and slushy and handed to him sitting down. Pick the seeds out of his watermelon wedge before he gets it, because a seed is throat-sized at this age, and the spitting target goes on a tray so the seeds land somewhere you can lift away rather than on the path he sits on. A metal tray out of the freezer sticks to wet hands, so it comes out on a dish towel. Keep the freezer door shut between scrapes, because he climbs and pulls now, and take the string down the moment the last peg comes off. The back step catches the sun all morning: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.
